html:
A set of land reforms in the Russian Empire led by the prime minister Pyotr Stolypin from 1906, which let peasants leave their village commune and own their land as private farms.

After the freeing of the serfs in 1861, most peasant land was held by the village commune, the mir. It shared out narrow strips in open fields and often redivided them, and members could not easily sell up or leave. Many officials blamed it for poor farming and rural unrest, which had exploded in the revolution of 1905.

A decree of November 1906 let peasants claim their strips as their own and join them into compact farms. A state bank lent money to buy land, and the government helped millions move to new farms in Siberia and Kazakhstan. Stolypin hoped to create a class of solid farmers loyal to the tsar. He also put down unrest harshly with field courts.

He was shot dead in Kyiv in 1911. By 1914 a minority of households had left the commune. The revolution of 1917 swept the reform away, and collectivisation later did the opposite.
sum: A set of land reforms in the Russian Empire led by the prime minister Pyotr Stolypin from 1906, which let peasants leave their village commune and own their land as private farms.
